Q: Devel::Cover interpreting hash access as false A:

How come $b{x} is seen as false by Devel::Cover?

Because there's a big in Devel::Cover. It only happens when it's the very last expression of a sub or the operand of return.

How can I make this pass as !l&&r?

By making it so // isn't the last op of the sub.

If you want to return $a or $b{x} as you are now:

{ $a // $b{x} }   # Or {; $a // $b{x} }

if ( 1 ) { $a // $b{x} }

do { $a // $b{x} }

my $rv = $a // $b{x}

If you just care whether it's true or false:

!!( $a // $b{x} )

Q: How do I use clock edge as selector for a mux? A:

As others mentioned, using clock as data is not common. A combinational mux be achieved using dwikle's answer, but if you really want to end up with flops (in that case out should be of type reg or logic, which is missing in your original code), then you can write:

always@(edge clk) 
begin
    unique case(clk)
        1'b0:    out <= in1;
        1'b1:    out <= in2;
    endcase
end

or equivalently you could use @(negedge clk or posedge clk) instead of edge. This may however, confuse your synthesis tool. Probably, the following is more straightforward:

always@(posedge clk) 
    out1 <= in1;
always@(negedge clk) 
    out2 <= in2;
assign out = clk ? out1 : out2;

Q: Non-standard header in HttpClient A:

No, at least not without reflection or rebuilding HttpClient.

The headers are set, even when using TryAddWithoutValidation, using internal methods which eventually reach HeaderDescriptor and KnownHeaders which does an OrdinalIgnoreCase lookup.

The afore-mentioned reflection would be something like this, note that this is obviously subject to breaking changes without notice.

private static readonly object _headerDescriptor = Activator.CreateInstance(
    typeof(HttpHeaders).Assembly.GetType("System.Net.Http.Headers.HeaderDescriptor"),
    BindingFlags.Instance | BindingFlags.NonPublic,
    null,
    ["Content-type", false],
    null);

private static readonly MethodInfo _tryAddWithoutValidation = typeof(HttpHeaders)
    .GetMethod(
        "TryAddWithoutValidation",
        BindingFlags.Instance | BindingFlags.NonPublic,
        [ _headerDescriptor.GetType(), typeof(string) ])
    ?? throw new Exception("Can't find TryAddWithoutValidation method");

public static void AddContenttype(this HttpHeaders headers, string value)
{
    _tryAddWithoutValidation.Invoke(headers, [ _headerDescriptor, value ]);
}

Do note that case-sensitive handling of HTTP headers is against the RFC 2616 specification and should be fixed:

4.2
...
Field names are case-insensitive.

Q: Why x86 doesn't have conditional predicated execution like ARM's IT / ITT, and why no link-register for return addresses? A:

I'm not quite convinced that this was due to transistor limitation though.

  • 4004 had 17x 4-bit registers and 4x 12-bit registers (including 3-level on-chip return stack which would be even better than single-level LR - except this is the WHOLE stack, there is no spillover to RAM) for total of 117 bits,
  • 4040 had 25x 4-bit registers and 8x 13 bit registers (7-level on-chip return stack - again this is the whole stack) for total of 205 bits
  • 8008 had 8x 8 bit registers and again 8x 14 bit registers with 7-level stack, for a total of 172 bits
  • 8080 had 8x 8 bit registers and 2x 16 bit registers for a measly 96 bits. It had an unlimited stack (first in the lineup to do so!), but it had none of hardware stack, not even LR. Surely they could've spared few transistors for a single register and hookups.

I'm not sure it would be so much better though. On one hand - faster leaf functions. I think 12 ticks at least are spent on stack memory access during call+return. On the other hand - non-leaf functions would have to save/restore LR manually, so that's at least 2 extra instruction bytes for each function, and thats 20 ticks I think. So it would make any sense to do LR only if they would expect leaf functions to be a majority, and maybe they didn't (after all, their customers demanded more than 7 levels of nesting!). Or maybe they just didn't want to complicate things with 2 different mechanisms.

Of course, they could've reintroduced LR in 8086, or in 80386 in 32-bit mode, or more realistically AMD could've done it when they designed 64-bit mode (which was long after all of the RISCs and ARM were a thing)... But they didn't.
